data.title: Human oversight in AI should be measured, not assumed
data.description:
RECENT reports in The Business Times have highlighted that clear permissions, audit trails, well-governed data and human sign-off on consequential decisions are key safeguards for financial institutions deploying artificial intelligence agents.

But keeping a human in the loop is not, by itself, a sufficient control. The more useful question is what risk that human checkpoint is meant to reduce, and whether it actually does so.

At the recent Global Finance & Technology Network session on AI innovation and governance, I asked a senior leader at a global bank whether an agent’s mandate could change in real time as conditions changed. The response was candid. It was a difficult question requiring further analysis.

That matters because human review can become a significant constraint as agentic workflows scale. McKinsey found that for a banking customer-service agent, human oversight accounted for 70 to 75 per cent of variable run costs, compared with 20 to 25 per cent for token costs.

The figures will differ across workflows, but they expose an important trade-off. Applying human approval too broadly can undermine the efficiency automation is meant to create.

Oversight should therefore follow the risk. A suspected fraud case, rejected loan, or large transfer to a new counterparty may warrant human judgment.

An agent assembling documents or updating an internal workflow within tightly defined permissions may not. The relevant factors include customer impact, value at risk, reversibility and uncertainty.

That principle is consistent with the AI risk-management guidelines from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), which urge financial institutions to apply controls proportionately according to their risk exposure and the scale and nature of their AI use.

MAS’ Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime Framework complements that direction with more granular guidance on how agent actions can be authorised, recorded and escalated for human review.

Banks should apply the same discipline to human oversight.

There is no single formula for assessing whether a checkpoint works. The industry will need evidence on where intervention catches material problems, changes proposed actions or adds delay without reducing risk.

A checkpoint may remain necessary for audit or accountability, even if interventions are rare.

The bank should be able to explain what risk it controls.

Crucially, this rule book cannot remain static. Agents act at machine speed, while the policies, mandates and controls governing them still change at human speed.

As agents take on new tasks, banks will need to revisit whether their escalation points still match the risks.

The goal is not maximum autonomy or maximum human involvement; it is to put human judgment where it changes the outcome. Every escalation should have a clear purpose.

Wei You Pan Field chief technology officer, MongoDB

data.title: Indonesian company taking over seized forest land is Danantara unit, document shows
data.description:
[JAKARTA] A new Indonesian company appointed to manage concessions seized last week from a subsidiary of a Singapore-based conglomerate is a unit of the country’s sovereign wealth fund Danantara, a document seen by Reuters showed.

The awarding of the concession is the latest sign of Danantara’s growing clout across Indonesia’s economy following its launch early last year, with hundreds of state firms worth more than US$1 trillion now under its control.

The move comes amid President Prabowo Subianto’s drive to increase state control over the country’s vast natural resources.

The government last week revoked the forest usage permits of Riau Andalan Pulp and Paper (Rapp), a unit of Singapore-headquartered Royal Golden Eagle, which cover 338,536 hectares (ha) of concessions in Riau province, citing fires and other violations.

On Tuesday (Nov 24), it was announced that the area would be managed by a previously unknown company called Garuda Adidaya Nusantara.

According to a law ministry document about the company reviewed by Reuters, Garuda Adidaya is 99 per cent controlled by Danantara Asset Management, and was established to engage in a wide range of forestry and plantation businesses as well as the processing of forest commodities.

It was established on Nov 19, the document showed, the same day the government issued the decree to revoke Rapp’s permits.

Neither the company’s status as a unit of Danantara nor the time when it was established has been previously reported.

Dozens of companies have been sanctioned in Indonesia this year as it battled its most intense forest fire season since 2015, with an estimated 2.9 million ha of land burned across the country between January and October 2026, indicated data from geomonitoring platform Nusantara Atlas.

The size of the fires that allegedly took place in Rapp’s concession remained unclear. Rapp said it had zero tolerance for burning and none of the fire incidents were caused by the company, adding that the majority of the outbreaks were suppressed within 24 hours.

Royal Golden Eagle belongs to one of Indonesia’s best-known billionaire tycoons, Sukanto Tanoto, making the Rapp seizure one of the highest-profile state takeovers.

“We respect the government’s authority and will continue to engage constructively with the relevant authorities,” a spokesperson for Rapp said on Wednesday, without responding to queries about the concession being run by Garuda Adidaya.

“Rapp firmly believes that it has operated in compliance with all applicable government regulatory requirements in the management of its forestry concessions.”

A call to Garuda Adidaya’s listed phone number was unanswered. Danantara did not respond to a request for comment.

The local government in Riau, where the concession is located, urged Garuda Adidaya and the central government’s forestry task force to provide clarity regarding the continuation of operations on the concession and the fate of its workers.

The task force has previously pledged that no Rapp employees would be laid off. REUTERS

data.title: ECB already had large support for rate hike in October, accounts show
data.description:
[FRANKFURT] European Central Bank policymakers were leaning towards an interest rate hike at their last meeting but opted for a delay to collect more evidence about inflation risks, the accounts of their Oct 28-29 meeting showed on Thursday (Nov 26).

The ECB debated a rate hike at the gathering but ultimately left rates unchanged, warning that inflation is likely to go higher than earlier thought, which may warrant further policy tightening.

“A large number of members noted that, as the incoming data since the September Governing Council meeting had confirmed the case for further policy tightening, they could have supported raising interest rates at the current meeting,” the ECB said in the accounts.

Policymakers agreed that second round effects of inflation have yet to materlialise but they still needed to preempt them.

“A hike at the current meeting would simply frontload the necessary monetary policy tightening,” the ECB said about the potential hike last month.

Most policymakers speaking on and off the record since that meeting have signalled that the Governing Council will hike rates by 25 basis points on Dec 17, suggesting such a move is all but a done deal.

The outlook further down the line is more murky, however, and few have provided guidance given that crucial wage negotiations between unions and employers, which have an outsized impact on future inflation, have yet to conclude.

Still, financial investors think the ECB is unlikely to be done in December since oil and gas prices are far above the ECB’s “baseline” scenario and a cold winter could push utility costs even higher given relatively low natural gas storage levels.

But inflation has yet to generate dangerous second-round effects, the labour market is softer than in the 2022 inflation episode and energy prices have recently retreated from highs that approached the “severe” scenario, indicating that any follow-up hike beyond December is not urgent.

Complicating the picture, the ECB will get new leadership in early 2027. ECB President Christine Lagarde and board member Isabel Schnabel are both leaving in the coming months, so a new president, most likely Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos, will have to preside over future rate hike debates. REUTERS

data.title: Asia has less to fear from the AI correction than you might think
data.description:
IN THE semiconductor manufacturing hubs of Taiwan and South Korea, financial regulators are worried about the mounting risks of the artificial-intelligence boom.

On Nov 19, Taiwan’s Financial Supervisory Commission tightened curbs on short selling to help stabilise the stock market, after its benchmark index suffered its sharpest weekly decline since 1991.

Meanwhile, South Korean policymakers are considering activating a 10.7 trillion won (US$8 billion) stock market stabilisation fund. The Kospi has lost a staggering 48 per cent since hitting a record high on Jun 22.

It is hard to overstate the impact of the AI infrastructure build-out on Asia’s economies. In 2024, seven of the top 10 exporters of AI-enabling goods were in Asia, including Singapore and Malaysia, the only South-east Asian economies with front-end chip manufacturing capabilities.

The Asia-Pacific’s share of global data centre capacity is expected to exceed 40 per cent by 2030. Within the region, South-east Asia accounts for the largest proportion of capacity under construction, led by Malaysia and Thailand.

Gone are the days when the technology-heavy US stock market had the highest AI concentration risk.

In the MSCI Asia Pacific ex-Japan index, the information technology and communication services sectors have a combined 46 per cent weighting.

Taiwan and South Korea alone account for nearly 50 per cent of the entire emerging market equity index.

Asia under scrutiny

The dramatic unravelling of the AI trade across global markets since early October has put Asia under intense scrutiny. A succession of shocks has fanned fears over the financing, regulation and geopolitics of the AI build-out.

The plunge in US tech shares, the angst over the scale of AI-related debt issuance, and the threat of a clampdown on US data centre construction following the decisive victory of the Democrats in the midterm elections have undermined confidence in the AI narrative.

Moreover, the spying scandal engulfing Nvidia has ensnared South-east Asia, as US authorities scrutinise alleged chip diversion to China through the region.

New rules unveiled by the US Commerce Department seek to close a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s cutting-edge AI chips remotely by renting computing power from South-east Asian data centres and cloud providers.

The Institute for Progress, a US think tank, estimates remote access will account for nearly one-third of China’s AI chip stock by the end of next year, with South-east Asia expected to comprise 72 per cent of China’s overseas AI compute.

HSBC says “efforts to restrict mainland China’s access to advanced technology could become a broader investment and demand shock for (South-east Asia).”

Not so fast. While Asia is acutely vulnerable to a slowdown in the AI investment cycle, the region foreshadowed the financial and regulatory risks of the boom, helping blunt the impact of the recent turmoil in the US tech sector.

South Korea’s equity market was the canary in the coal mine for the AI trade. Foreign funds had already dumped US$130 billion of the country’s stocks in 2026 prior to the sell-off in the US, contributing to steep declines in Asian tech shares over the summer. This has made the region’s equity markets look increasingly undervalued, especially given the enduring strength of corporate earnings.

In a sign of the degree to which AI demand remains exceptionally buoyant, Goldman Sachs expects profit growth for the Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index in 2027 to reach 26 per cent, driven by the tech hardware and chip sectors in South Korea and Taiwan.

Regulatory realities

Furthermore, fears about the impact of tougher regulatory scrutiny of the AI build-out on South-east Asia’s economies are overdone.

While the new US-export licensing rules will test regional operators in the near term, the region has benefited from restrictions on data centre development designed to ensure the boom does not turn to bust.

Singapore’s full-blown moratorium on new construction in 2019 to 2022 was a catalyst for the surge in investment in the Malaysian state of Johor, currently the largest data centre market in the Asia-Pacific when combining operational and planned capacity.

It was also the precursor to the imposition of regulations across South-east Asia designed to balance sustainability requirements with digital infrastructure needs, creating a more resilient data centre market. The region’s neutrality, moreover, cuts both ways.

While many anchor tenants of data centres in Malaysia and Thailand are Chinese, a large portion is American. This “could divert more incremental demand towards (Malaysia) if (data centre) regulations tighten in the US”, notes Citigroup.

Lastly, it is important to put the threats to the AI build-out into perspective.

First, non-AI workloads – traditional compute and cloud services – accounted for nearly half of global data centre demand in 2025, said McKinsey.

In Asia, where digital infrastructure is at an earlier stage of the growth cycle, the share was much higher. Strong domestic and regional demand provide a buffer against a slowdown in the AI capital expenditure cycle.

Second, anti-data centre politicians’ bark is worse than their bite. In the US, Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic governor-elect of Texas – which accounts for one quarter of the nation’s planned data centre capacity – said construction of facilities with permits will be allowed to proceed.

In fact, stricter rules for approving new data centres should help ease concern over the financing of the AI boom. A slower, more expensive and selective build-out will increase the value of existing AI data centres, as the mismatch between strong demand and supply constraints intensifies.

Third, portfolio diversification in the age of AI is easier said than done, particularly in Asia.

While India is touted as the “anti-AI trade” because of its limited exposure to tech hardware, many fund managers see this as a liability and believe AI capital expenditure and monetisation will continue to drive returns in Asian equity markets.

The AI narrative remains compelling.

That Nvidia, under pressure from US President Donald Trump, reinstated the scandal-tainted Jensen Huang as its CEO shows that the build-out has a strong political backstop – one that limits how far lawmakers can let the AI trade unwind without hurting tens of trillions of dollars in American retirement savings.

Asia’s crucial role in the AI supply chain makes it a key gauge of investor sentiment. More volatility is inevitable. All the more reason not to lose sight of the powerful drivers of the region’s digital infrastructure boom.

The writer is an independent adviser and columnist

data.title: Stocks to watch: Kimly, AP Oil, Heptamax
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 26):

Kimly : The coffee shop operator reported a 30.8 per cent fall in net profit to S$12.8 million for its second half ended Sep 30, from S$18.5 million a year earlier. Revenue came in 1 per cent lower at S$161.1 million, from S$162.8 million previously. Kimly proposed a final dividend of S$0.01 a share for H2, bringing the total FY2026 dividend to S$0.02 a share. Shares of Kimly ended flat at S$0.365 on Wednesday, before the news.

AP Oil : The CEO of the petroleum products company, Ho Chee Hon, was sentenced to six months jail and a fine of S$25,000 for drink-driving on Wednesday. Accordingly, he will be away on a leave of absence for a period of six months from Dec 1. The company said that the charges are personal in nature and unrelated to its business or operations. Its board added that Ho remains suitable to continue in his role as CEO. Shares of AP Oil ended flat at S$0.126 on Wednesday, before the update.

Heptamax : The industrial solutions company, which is proposing to buy a data centre company for S$500 million in a reverse takeover, has been queried by the Singapore Exchange Regulation over the deal. Among other things, the regulator asked how the valuation for the target company Racks Central was arrived at. It also asked Heptamax to give details of the beneficial owners of the vendor. The company replied that the price was arrived at on a willing-buyer, willing-seller basis, taking into account Racks Central’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation for FY2025, among other things. Heptamax ended flat at S$0.131 on Wednesday.

data.title: Japan firms say rate hikes are starting to bite, new study shows
data.description:
JAPANESE businesses are increasingly feeling the weight of rising interest rates, a new survey showed, sending a fresh reminder to the Bank of Japan of the need to keep a careful eye on financial conditions.

Almost 59 per cent of companies said the negative effects of higher rates are greater than the positive ones, according to the survey released on Wednesday (Nov 25) by the Teikoku Databank. That’s an increase of 14 percentage points from the previous poll in December. 

The BOJ raised its benchmark rate to the highest level in three decades in September and it’s widely expected to hike again next month.

Governor Kazuo Ueda’s board has raised policy rates six times since 2024, though its benchmark is still among the lowest among major economies at 1.25 per cent. 

The latest survey data shows the impact of those hikes is spreading across the corporate sector. It suggests the BOJ will continue to carefully watch both the accumulated impact of rate hikes and the upside risks to inflation, which has climbed above the central bank’s 2 per cent target. 

The Teikoku Databank found that some 48 per cent of companies said their main banks had approached them about raising lending rates. Out of those firms, 29 per cent said their rates had already been increased.

Average rates on new loans rose to 2.12 per cent in September, according to a separate BOJ report released on Wednesday, the highest level since 1996. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Malaysia government likely to serve full term, Anwar aide says
data.description:
MALAYSIAN Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government is likely to serve until the end of its term despite recent speculation over an early election, according to his senior political adviser Zafrul Aziz.

“I believe so,” Zafrul said when asked in a Bloomberg TV interview with Haslinda Amin whether the government would last a full term. “We have commitments from all our coalition partners that we want the government to continue until its full term,” he said, adding that the timing ultimately depends on the prime minister.

Malaysia’s parliament is due to complete its five-year term in December 2027, with an election required within 60 days of its dissolution.

Speculation over an earlier vote has nevertheless persisted, with Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi repeatedly calling for polls to be brought forward. Anwar has said he would consider such calls, while stressing that his multi-party government remains stable.

Responding to a question on US chip restrictions, Zafrul, who held the finance and trade portfolios under two different governments and who is also chair of the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, said the key issues were whether advanced semiconductors are ending up with unauthorised users and whether the companies using them are approved. 

Malaysia would give Washington its “full cooperation” to ensure the country remains a credible and attractive location for data centres, he said.

Zafrul said the new US restrictions, which impose licensing requirements on shipments of advanced AI chips to Malaysia and tighten controls on overseas computing access, are likely to affect some companies investing in Malaysia’s data-center industry, though it is too early to determine the scale of the impact.

“My guess will be yes,” he said when asked whether the measures could affect investment. “There will be some companies obviously affected by this.”

Companies seeking access to US chips would need to comply with Washington’s rules, he added.

His comments come as Malaysia’s role in the AI supply chain faces increased scrutiny. The US Commerce Department this week added Singapore-based Megaspeed International and six related entities to its trade blacklist, citing a “significant risk” they could be involved in diverting advanced computing products to unauthorized users or uses. Two of the entities, Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd. and MSFusion Sdn Bhd., are in Malaysia.

US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips.

Malaysia is separately investigating whether chips imported by Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed unit, were subsequently re-exported and whether any such shipments complied with Malaysian law. Megaspeed has said it takes its US compliance obligations “extremely seriously.”

The scrutiny comes as data centres have become an increasingly important source of investment for Malaysia.

The country approved RM123.5 billion (US$30 billion) of data-centre and cloud-computing projects in the first nine months of 2026, up 44.5 per cent from a year earlier and equivalent to more than a third of all approved investment during the period, according to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority.

Zafrul said Malaysia’s data centre expansion has already exceeded the government’s expectations, while stressing the need to preserve the country’s credibility with investors.

Electrical and electronics investment jumped 85.3 per cent in the first nine months from a year earlier to RM40.8 billion, according to MIDA, underscoring the growing importance of technology investment to the economy.

“For us to continue to be an attractive location for data centres, we need to make sure that our institutions are credible enough for them to then operate here,” Zafrul said. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: OCBC, Manulife US Reit
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Tuesday (Nov 24):

OCBC : The bank has appointed Ang Eng Siong, the current CEO of OCBC China, as its new head of global corporate banking from Jan 1, 2027. The appointment comes as the bank reorganises its wholesale banking business into three divisions. Under the new structure, Ang will lead what OCBC calls “GWB 1”, focusing on scaling the large corporate segment in its core markets – Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Greater China – as well as its overseas branches. Shares of OCBC closed 0.5 per cent or S$0.13 lower at S$26.41 on Monday, before the announcement.

Manulife US Real estate investment trust (Reit) : The trust manager said that it has negotiated a proposed agreement with its lenders that would allow it to exit a three-year debt restructuring and resume distributions to unitholders. The agreement is subject to unitholders’ passing resolutions at a Dec 15 extraordinary general meeting. Under the agreement, lenders would waive certain conditions under the Reit’s 2023 master restructuring agreement, and extend loans by about 12 to 18 months, excluding the sponsor-lender loan. Units of the trust ended flat at US$0.031 before the announcement.

Trading halt: Keppel and Starhub called for a trading halt on Tuesday morning, pending the release of an announcement. StarHub then announced that it has agreed to merge with Keppel’s M1 in an all-share deal. It also exercised an option to buy Circles Life’s Singapore mobile business. Shares of Keppel closed S$0.02 or 0.2 per cent lower at S$8.83 on Monday, while shares of StarHub closed S$0.01 or 1 per cent lower at S$1.01.

data.title: Singapore business groups contest US overcapacity claims, flag risks to investment and hiring
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore business groups pushed back on Thursday (Nov 26) against US claims that the Republic’s policies contribute to excess manufacturing capacity.

Proposed US tariffs of up to 20 per cent could both erode manufacturers’ competitiveness and unfairly influence where companies invest and produce, they warned.

The Singapore Business Federation (SBF) said it was “disappointed” by the content of a report released a day earlier by the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR).

“We do not believe the findings accurately reflect Singapore’s market-driven economy, our role as a global trading and logistics hub, or the mutually beneficial nature of US-Singapore economic relations,” SBF said.

It added the US has consistently run a trade surplus with Singapore, reaching about US$33.3 billion in 2025, including surpluses in sectors cited in the investigation, including semiconductors, electrical equipment and petrochemicals. 

SBF noted that global demand drives manufacturing investment in Singapore, and rejected the criticism that the Republic’s industrial policies, which focus on raising productivity and competitiveness, sustain “idle or uneconomic capacity”.

The Singapore Semiconductor Industry Association (SSIA) also disputed the finding that Singapore’s support for chipmakers contributed to structural overcapacity.

Growth in manufacturing capacity should not necessarily be equated with structural overcapacity, executive director Ang Wee Seng told The Business Times.

Eroding Singapore’s competitiveness 

SBF also warned that a lack of parity across the tariff rates proposed for different economies could affect Singapore firms’ competitiveness and shape investment, production and supply chain decisions.

“We recognise that there remains room for further negotiations,” the federation said, adding that it hoped talks would take into account Singapore’s circumstances as a small, open economy.

Singapore Manufacturing Federation (SMF) group CEO Wayne Yap said that the proposed tariffs could “further erode manufacturers’ competitiveness”.

SMF found in a recent poll that more than eight in 10 respondents already expect operating costs to rise in 2027; Yap said any additional tariffs could further squeeze margins, as well as affect investment and hiring. 

He flagged the precision engineering components, industrial equipment, medical devices, plastics and processed food industries as vulnerable, with exposure varying by product.

Some 65 per cent of SMF members have already reported direct or indirect exposure to US tariffs and other trade measures, with 59 per cent of these companies reporting lower revenue in 2026 due to tariffs or trade disruptions.

“Manufacturers cannot continue absorbing additional costs without consequences for Singapore’s manufacturing competitiveness,” said Yap.

Though proposed exemptions for chips, chipmaking equipment and certain parts offered SSIA’s Ang some reassurance, he highlighted that the semiconductor industry “operates within a highly interconnected global ecosystem”. 

Tariffs affecting downstream products such as electronics, automotive systems, industrial equipment and data centre infrastructure can influence overall semiconductor demand, he noted, while duties on unexempted goods could also raise costs and complicate supply chain planning for smaller equipment, materials and precision engineering suppliers.

Feedback wanted 

Ang acknowledged that it is too early to assess the impact on individual companies, as semiconductor investments take years to plan and require substantial capital. The USTR has yet to specify when the proposed tariffs will take effect.

“Prolonged uncertainty could influence the pace and timing of investment, capacity expansion and hiring decisions,” he said.

Companies told BT that their exposure to the US varies. 

Mainboard-listed Addvalue Technologies , which develops satellite communications equipment, counts the US as an important market.

CEO Tan Khai Pang observed that the US is also important to the “inherently global” satellite communications and space industry and its “highly specialised technology and supply chains”. 

On the other hand, Ray Goh, general manager of mainboard-listed semiconductor and electronics equipment supplier Ellipsiz , expects limited direct impact.

The company distributes equipment and supplies across the Asia-Pacific, including some equipment imported from the US, and does not ship goods there.

The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry has encouraged affected companies to share their concerns; SBF, SSIA and SMF confirmed to BT that they will consult businesses to assess exposure, share feedback with the government and offer advice.

“While we cannot control developments in the global trade environment, we can determine how we respond,” said SBF CEO Kok Ping Soon.

“Our businesses must continue to remain agile, adapt to changing circumstances and actively seek out new opportunities.”

data.title: Peach Blossoms comes into full bloom with latest revamp
data.description:
Restaurant revamp

Peach Blossoms Level 5, Parkroyal Collection, Marina Bay 6 Raffles Boulevard Singapore 039594 Tel: 6845-1118 Open daily for lunch and dinner: 12 pm to 3 pm; 6.30 pm to 10.30 pm. Open at 11.30 am on Saturday and Sunday.

SOMETHING happened to Edward Chong.

He grew up.

To us, he was always the wunderkind of modern Chinese cooking in Singapore – with one hand on his Harry Potter wok of wizardry, and the other permanently poised over the “kitschy crockery” tab on Taobao.

There was no culinary convention he wouldn’t challenge. Psychedelic dimsum, crushed frozen roses over yusheng, jiggly pig jellies – everything was fair game. With ideas flowing faster than he could cook them, you rarely saw the same dish twice.

But those were the days when Peach Blossoms still had something to prove, with Chong’s cooking impactful if a little on the wild side. Now with a few accolades under his belt – and a major kitchen renovation done and dusted – he’s traded in his young maverick status for cool ajusshi confidence.

Then again, growing up doesn’t mean playing it safe. Chong is still gleefully genre-bending, as seen from an airy spring roll streaked with squid ink tiger stripes and served with caviar. Where it sits in the lexicon of Singapore-inspired Chinese cuisine, is another matter.

At S$88, you pay more for the little tin of caviar than the fried popiah parcel, an engineering marvel of wafer-thin skin that shatters uncontrollably at first bite. There’s creamy otah mousse inside, and a convenient air pocket to fill with caviar. We don’t know how, but this piping-hot, spicy, salty crunch-fest actually works. 

Chong can get carried away sometimes, and his combination platter (S$48) is as unnecessarily fussy as the cloud of dry ice billowing over it. Chicken rice and cured hamachi are great separately, but awkward as lift strangers when forced into a tart shell. Fried siewmai stuffed with otah and drizzled with mentaiko mayo leaves nothing to the imagination, while Peking duck and foie gras moulded into a canape barely raises an eyebrow. It takes a squid ink tart with the crunch of diced jicama and the clean flavour of squid to bring us back to attention. 

But other than this, there’s a newfound restraint in Chong’s menu, where the Hakka chef sticks closer to the Cantonese and other dialect playbooks than his own imagination.

Any fatigue from a long work day evaporates from the first sip of double-boiled spring chicken, cordyceps and Jeju abalone soup (S$58) – a consomme that’s clear as day and steeped in goodness. Abalone and slippery fish maw give you something to chew, while cordyceps show up as proof of ingredient.

Pork tripe and white peppercorn (S$38) are best pals in a milky, heartwarming brew with the gentle heat of pepper to balance the richness.

Malaysian ducks should claim Chong as a national hero for his smoked duck with the sweet scent of angelica (S$48 for half). It boasts the juiciness of meat that has never felt conflict in its life – just supple tenderness infused with a gentle smokiness, covered with golden burnished skin.

Chong also shows off elevated zichar skill with his version of mapo dofu (S$48) – steamed egg custard topped with spicy tofu and tender slices of wagyu. It’s spicy and in-your-face, but with a bowl of white rice it’s a complete, homespun meal. 

It’s the same with seafood vermicelli (S$68), essentially hor fun with thin noodles, in an egg-enriched gravy with fleshy, muscular prawns. At this point, kudos go to our server Hailey whose spot-on recommendations show off some gems that we would otherwise have missed.

Chong’s dry ice fetish comes into play again with dessert. This time, it spews from a miniature melon filled with monkfruit jelly, peach resin, ice cream and balls of Charentais melon. At S$58, it’s an ambitious combination let down by the nondescript melon and jelly.

It takes a simple hot peanut broth with a single glutinous rice dumpling (S$22) to give us the ideal sweet ending.

With its refreshed surroundings and a menu that leans closer to tradition without sacrificing Chong’s unique flair, Peach Blossoms has come into its own. It can be pricey, and Chong’s penchant for strong, salty and robust flavours can overwhelm some palates. But he’s come a long way and he’s right where he should be.

Rating: 7.5
